messages:
alex: FYI after the maintenance drain of several gpu nodes in us-west-edge we're observing intermittent 503s from inference clients, looks like some headless backends stopped answering
jamal: same, saw a spike of grpc timeouts around 12:03 PDT in the LB logs
infra-bot: automated-drain completed for node gpu-edge-12 at 2026-03-18T12:01:40Z
sophia: quick check -> endpointslice for infer-svc looks inconsistent, posting output
sophia: ```
NAME                       ADDRESSTYPE   ENDPOINTS   PORTS
infer-svc-0001             IPv4          0/6         8080
infer-svc-0002             IPv4          4/6         8080
```
ben: 0/6 on a primary slice. could be endpoint-slice controller lagging behind the node drain
sophia: apiserver metrics show etcd write latency spiked during the drain window, endpoint-slice-controller queue_depth shot up
harry: if the controller lags we can end up with partial slice state, kube-proxy may still program iptables for removed endpoints - blackholing traffic
jamal: example SRV lookup failing intermittently: dig +short SRV _grpc._tcp.infer-svc.namespace.svc.cluster.local -> sometimes returns nothing
sophia: grabbed kube-proxy logs from gpu-edge-13, seeing errors on programming endpoints
sophia: ```
E0318 12:04:12.345678   12345 proxier.go:1104] Failed to add endpoints for service infer-svc: iptables failed: exit status 1
I0318 12:04:12.345689   12345 proxier.go:876] Service infer-svc had stale endpoints, continuing
```
alex: confirmed a handful of nodes kept iptables rules targeting addresses that were removed during the drain. conntrack entries pointing at those IPs cause requests to hang
ben: short-term mitigation: restart kube-proxy on affected nodes and flush conntrack. will briefly disrupt in-flight connections but clears stale NAT rules
sophia: scaled endpoint-slice-controller from 2 -> 4 replicas in control-plane autoscaler to give it headroom during upcoming drains
harry: long-term we should throttle node evictions for inference pools, or prefer eviction targets in other AZs first. also consider backpressure in the controller when mass node removals are scheduled
ajam: (typo) jamal: running the kube-proxy restarts on the four impacted nodes now, will post results
ben: snippet used to find stale iptables rules:
ben: ```bash
kubectl get pods -n kube-system -l k8s-app=kube-proxy -o wide
ssh node
sudo iptables -t nat -S | grep <old-endpoint-ip>
```
alex: created INC-2026-042, priority P2, tagging eng-infra and eng-runtime. runbook steps in the ticket:
alex: 1) identify nodes with stale iptables rules via sudo iptables -t nat -S | grep <removed-ip>
alex: 2) systemctl restart kube-proxy on affected nodes (or kubectl rollout restart ds/kube-proxy -n kube-system)
alex: 3) flush conntrack: sudo conntrack -D -d <removed-ip>
alex: 4) monitor endpointslice counts and coreDNS SRV query success
kube-bot: incident INC-2026-042 created by alex, severity P2, channel #eng-infra
sophia: after restarts endpointslices converged -> all slices show full endpoints again, coreDNS SRV queries return expected records, client errors dropped back to baseline at ~12:19 PDT
jamal: post-restart checks look green; keeping incident open for RCA and follow-up actions
harry: filing follow-up items: adjust drain cadence for gpu pools, add controller autoscaler buffer, add alert on endpoint-slice-controller queue depth and apiserver etcd write latency spikes
alex: agree. also adding a note to staging runbook to sequence node drains with controller scaling so we don't overwhelm control plane during large maintenance windows
sophia: opened a PR to the controller operator to allow a transient 30s batching window during scheduled maintenance updates (WIP)
ben: thanks everyone, good catch on the iptables/conntrack angle. will add a short KB entry on how to detect this to the eng-infra runbooks
alex: last check 12:35 PDT - endpoints stable and client QoS normal, leaving incident open for final RCA doc
